Study design: RCT

characteristics.name: Participants
characteristics.value:
Sample size: total: 33, IG: Maitland mobilisation 17, CG: Mulligan mobilisation 16 

Method of recruitment: participants were recruited from physiotherapy and rehabilitation clinic of the university where the study was conducted.

Setting: physiotherapy and rehabilitation clinic of the university

Country: India

Baseline characteristics

  • Age in years, mean (SD): IG: 35.4 (3.71); CG 35.3 (3.13)
  • Sex, number (%) women: not reported

Duration of LBP:  > 12 weeks for the population, not further specified

Inclusion criteria

  • Males and females aged between 20 and 45 years
  • Suffering from low back pain for more than 12 weeks, with or without leg pain above the knee, 
  • Pain on numeric pain rating scale (NPRS) > 3/10 
  • Back pain elicited or increased by active lumbar flexion or extension movement, and pain elicited by application of PA force on one or more lumbar vertebra

Exclusion criteria

  • Subjects with any previous surgery of the spine
  • History of spondylosis
  • Spondylolisthesis
  • Spine tumors
  • Cauda equina syndrome
  • Signs of neurological deficit
  • Slipped intervertebral discs
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Spinal infection
  • Pregnancy

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Maitland mobilisation 

  • Description: 'subjects in group 1 received Maitland mobilization with central and unilateral posteroanterior (PA) glide on the lumbar vertebra which was hypomobile depending on the clinical finding. During mobilization of the lumbar spine, the patient was in a prone position with their hands by their sides on the treatment table, and the head turned comfortably to one side. The grades used were based on severity and irritability of the condition at the discretion of the therapist.' 
  • Non-SMT component: 'general exercises for the spine, abdomen, lower limbs, specific and localized exercises for the spinal segments and pelvic girdle in each treatment session. The purpose was mainly to mobilize hypomobile areas or to stretch paravertebral muscle tissue. The exercises were performed by doing 2 or 3 sets of 10-15 repetitions for each exercise, with 30 sec to 1min rest between each set.'
  • Duration/dose: 3 cycles of 60 seconds were applied at the hypomobile intervertebral level with a 1 min rest period. 16 sessions on 4 weeks.
  • Treatment provider: not reported

CG: Mulligan mobilisation

  • Description: 'The subjects in group 2 received SNAGs applied either centrally or unilaterally, to the symptomatic spinal levels with active lumbar flexion.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'general exercises for the spine, abdomen, lower limbs, specific and localized exercises for the spinal segments, and pelvic girdle in each treatment session. The purpose was mainly to mobilize hypomobile areas or to stretch paravertebral muscle tissue. The exercises were performed by doing 2 or 3 sets of 10-15 repetitions for each exercise, with 30 sec to 1min rest between each set.'
  • Duration/dose: Each SNAG was sustained for few seconds at the end of range of flexion. 2 to 3 sets of 4-6 repetitions were performed
  • Treatment provider: not reported

characteristics.name: Outcomes
characteristics.value:
Critical outcomes: 

Pain: NPRS (0-10). Subjects were asked to rate their current level of pain, as well as their worst and least amounts of pain in the past 24 h. The average of the 3 ratings represented the level of pain of the subject at that time point.

Functional status: ODI

Recovery: not reported

Important outcomes: lumbar flexion and extension range of motion and EMG at L3 and L5

Adverse events: not reported

Follow up: 4 weeks

characteristics.name: Notes
characteristics.value:
Authors' results and conclusion: 'The study reveals that addition of either Maitland or Mulligan mobilization techniques of the spine does not show a difference in the improvement of symptoms associated with non-specific chronic low back pain.'

Funding source: no funding was received

Declarations of interest: none to declare

characteristics.name: Participants
characteristics.value:
Sample size: total: 42, IG: SMT plus active exercise 22, CG:  detuned ultrasound plus active exercise 20

Method of recruitment: those subjects presenting for care

Setting: one rheumatology clinic at a university hospital

Country: Switzerland

Baseline characteristics

  • Age in years, mean (SD): IG 44 (12); CG 42 (12)
  • Sex, number (%) women: IG 36%; CG 30%

Duration of LBP: not reported, but > 12 weeks for the population.

Inclusion criteria 

  • Non-specific LBP with or without symptoms in the lower extremity for a period of 12 to 26 weeks'
  • Age 20-65 years.

Exclusion criteria

  • Spinal fracture or surgery within the previous 6 months
  • Pregnancy
  • Neoplasia
  • Spinal infection
  • Spinal inflammatory arthritis
  • Low back pain of visceral origin
  • Severe sensitive and/or motor radicular deficit from nerve root origin of less than 6 months
  • Score of 3/5 or more on the Waddell Score
  • On sick leave from work for 6 months or more
  • Psychiatric disorders
  • Opioid medication
  • Patient unable to collaborate (linguistic barrier; cognitive impairments)
  • Radiologic abnormalities other than degenerative disease
  • Clinical neurogenic claudication.'

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: SMT plus active exercise  

  • Description: 'One (or more) of the following techniques was used: a.) Passive accessory intervertebral movements: a central or unilateral posteroanterior pressure applied on painful or stiffed vertebral segment(s) with the patient lying prone; b.) Muscle-energy techniques: a hold-relaxed technique performed on an ilium dysfunction with the patient side-lying; c.) high-velocity, low-amplitude dynamic thrust (manipulation): a rotational-lateral flexion thrust performed on a stiffed vertebral segment(s) with the patient side lying.
  • Non-SMT component:  'Active exercise consisted of the following: 1.) Mobility exercises: to be performed throughout the 8 therapeutic sessions in order to improve the patient’s spinal range of motion and pain; 2.) Pelvic tilt and low back lateral flexion exercises; 3.) Passive stretching exercises given following the 2nd session; and 4.) Motor control exercises were given at the 4th session for active recruitment of stabilizing trunk muscles. The physiotherapy evaluation (45 minutes) included: a standard physiotherapy assessment for non-specific low back pain; 2) educational information on the low back anatomy and biomechanics, ways to protect the spine during activities of daily living and rest during episodes of pain (presented in a 6-page booklet); 3) 2 home mobility exercises (pelvic tilt and low back lateral flexion, in supine), to be performed twice a day, 2 sets of 10 repetitions. After the 3rd or 4th therapeutic session, the recommendation of home exercises changed to stretching and motor control exercises (see active exercises for dosage and progression). Home exercises were reviewed at the beginning of each therapeutic session and recorded daily by patients in a diary.'
  • Duration/dose: 'The therapeutic sessions (30 minutes) consisted of 5 to 10 minutes of MT intervention followed by active exercises. Treatments consisted of a physiotherapy evaluation and 8 therapeutic sessions (1–2 sessions per week) over a period of 4 to 8 weeks.'
  • Treatment provider: performed by a single physiotherapist with 15 years of experience

CG: detuned ultrasound plus active exercise

  • Description: 'relied on detuned ultrasound on the patient’s painful and/or inflammatory site.  Active exercise consisted of the following: 1.) Mobility exercises: to be performed throughout the 8 therapeutic sessions in order to improve the patient’s spinal range of motion and pain; 2.) Pelvic tilt and low back lateral flexion exercises; 3.) Passive stretching exercises given following the 2nd session; and 4.) Motor control exercises were given at the 4th session for active recruitment of stabilizing trunk muscles. The physiotherapy evaluation (45 minutes) included: a standard physiotherapy assessment for non-specific low back pain; 2) educational information on the low back anatomy and biomechanics, ways to protect the spine during activities of daily living and rest during episodes of pain (presented in a 6-page booklet); 3) 2 home mobility exercises (pelvic tilt and low back lateral flexion, in supine), to be performed twice a day, 2 sets of 10 repetitions. After the 3rd or 4th therapeutic session, the recommendation of home exercises changed to stretching and motor control exercises (see active exercises for dosage and progression). Home exercises were reviewed at the beginning of each therapeutic session and recorded daily by patients in a diary.'
  • Duration/dose: 'The therapeutic sessions (30 minutes) consisted of detuned ultrasound followed by active exercises. Treatments consisted of a physiotherapy evaluation and 8 therapeutic sessions (1–2 sessions per week) over a period of 4 to 8 weeks.'
  • Treatment provider: delivered by 2 physiotherapists with 5 and 25 years of working experience at the rheumatology unit.

characteristics.name: Outcomes
characteristics.value:
Critical outcomes: 

Pain: VAS (0-10). Subjects were asked to rate their average pain during the last 48 hours and current pain 

Functional status: ODI

Recovery: not reported

Important outcomes:  FABQ (subscales: a four-item physical activity subscale (FABQ-pa) and seven-item work subscale (FABQ-wk), Sorensen test (evaluates the erector spinae muscles endurance) and Shirado test (assesses the abdominal muscles endurance).

Adverse events: any adverse event

Follow up: following the 8th therapeutic session, and at 3- and 6 months after the end of treatment

characteristics.name: Notes
characteristics.value:
Authors' results and conclusion: 'This study confirmed the immediate analgesic effect of manual therapy over sham therapy. Followed by specific active exercises, it reduces significantly functional disability and tends to induce a larger decrease in pain intensity compared to the control group.' '...This study provides insufficient evidence for an effect of manual therapy on FABQ-wk, FABQ-pa, or Sorensen scores.'

Funding source: DO-RE Funds of the Swiss National Science Foundation (13DPD3-109903).

Declarations of interest: none to declare.

Comments reviewer: The population was smaller than estimated prior to the study. The authors calculated that 52 patients per group were needed (i.e. 104 in total), but only 42 were recruited. Additionally, patient recruitment was provided exclusively by one rheumatology clinic at a university hospital; therefore, the findings might be limited for non-specific LBP. The authors note, 'This may have contributed in selecting patients with more inflammatory signs and higher severity of disease; however, strict criteria of selection.... were used in order to exclude patients with a bad prognosis...'

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: 'Following the initial evaluation visit, patients were randomly assigned to their treatment group. Concealment allocation was performed by using a randomized table of numbers, from which every four consecutive numbers were retained. Individual index cards with the corresponding number were folded and placed in consecutively numbered, sealed opaque envelopes. Even numbers were allocated to the manual therapy (MT) group and odd numbers to the sham therapy (ST) group.'
'A physiotherapist not involved in the patients’ therapies and blinded to the treatment groups was responsible for the treatment allocation.'

Trial registration number: NCT01496144. Pain (11-point VAS) is listed as the primary outcome and FABQ as the secondary outcome. No other outcomes were described in the protocol, although functional status (ODI) was measured and presented as a primary outcome.
Age, gender, duration of back pain and ODI are similar. There is a baseline difference in VAS score between the groups (65 and 53 (sham and MT, respectively)).

Follow up: Post-treatment (following the 8th therapeutic session), and at 3- and 6 months after end of treatment. Comment: the timing of the therapy sessions was similar per group.

characteristics.name: Participants
characteristics.value:
Sample size: total: 110, IG: SMT 28, CG1: standard SMT placebo 27, CG2: enhanced SMT placebo group 27, CG3: no-treatment control 28

Setting: University of Florida and Health Science Center

Method of recruitment: advertisement

Country: USA

Baseline Characteristics

  • Age in years, mean (SD): Overall: 31.68 (11.85); IG: 32.07 (10.98); CG1: 33.22 (13.29); CG2: 31.56 (11.85); CG3: 29.85 (12.09)
  • Sex, number (%) women: Overall: 70%; IG: 75%; CG1: 63%; CG2: 74%; CG3: 68.0%

Duration of LBP: in weeks, median (interquartile range): Overall 16.03 (153); IG: 12 (164.50); CG1: 24 (100); CG2: 36 (543); CG3:(108) 

Duration of LBP was not a consideration for inclusion/exclusion from the study because we wished to include a full range of individuals with LBP for ecological validity, whereas anticipating individuals with LBP more chronic in nature would predominate because of our recruitment strategy. 

Inclusion criteria

  • Participants between the ages of 18 and 60
  • Currently experiencing mechanical LBP ≥ 4/10 at its worst over the past 24 hours on a NPRS

Exclusion criteria

  • Pain or paraesthesia below the knees
  • Potential non-musculoskeletal causes of LBP as indicated by unexplained weight loss of greater than 10 pounds, fever corresponding to LBP, non-mechanical pain, and bowel or bladder dysfunction 
  • Surgery to the low back within the past 6 months
  • Systemic illness known to affect sensation, that is, diabetes
  • Chronic pain condition unrelated to LBP
  • Fracture as the cause of LBP
  • Pregnancy

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
'All participants receiving the SMT were instructed through the informed consent process that they would receive either a studied SMT or a placebo intervention and were provided no additional information regarding which intervention they received.'

IG: SMT 

  • Description: 'The SMT group received an SMT previously shown to be effective in the treatment of some individuals experiencing LBP. The SMT was performed 2 times on each side.'
  • Non-SMT component: none
  • Duration/dose: 'Participants receiving the SMT and both placebo groups were scheduled for 5 additional sessions during the next 2 weeks to receive their assigned intervention.'
  • Treatment provider: two licensed physical therapists

CG1: standard SMT vs sham SMT, described as placebo SMT by trialists 

  • Description: 'The standard SMT placebo group received a placebo SMT. The novel placebo was intended to mimic the studied SMT; however, it differed biomechanically. A thrust of similar force to the studied SMT was then applied to the contralateral anterior superior iliac spine of the pelvis directly into the table. Additionally, the applied load was to a spine positioned vastly differently from typical clinical practice and not done with therapeutic intent. The placebo SMT was performed 2 times on each side.'
  • Non-SMT component: none
  • Duration/dose: 'Participants receiving the SMT and both placebo groups were scheduled for 5 additional sessions during the next 2 weeks to receive their assigned intervention.'
  • Treatment provider: two licensed physical therapists

CG2: Enhanced SMT vs sham SMT, described as placebo SMT by trialists

  • Description: 'The enhanced SMT placebo group received the same placebo as the standard placebo group. They were told, 'The manual therapy technique you will receive has been shown to significantly reduce low back pain in some people' immediately prior to the first intervention and subsequent intervention sessions. The enhanced placebo SMT group received the placebo SMT 2 times on each side.'
  • Non-SMT component: none
  • Duration/dose: 'Participants receiving the SMT and both placebo groups were scheduled for 5 additional sessions during the next 2 weeks to receive their assigned intervention.'
  • Treatment provider: two licensed physical therapists

CG3: No treatment control

  • Description: 'sat quietly for 5 minutes during the initial session.'
  • Duration/dose: not applicable
  • Treatment provider: not applicable

characteristics.name: Outcomes
characteristics.value:
Critical outcomes: 

Pain:  NPRS (0-100) pain intensity ('usual pain over the past week')

Functional status: ODI

Recovery: not reported

Important outcomes: participant satisfaction, believability of the placebo, and pain sensitivity was assessed in various manners immediately following treatment: mechanical pain sensitivity (quantified through a mechanical VAS 0-100), thermal pain sensitivity (using the Medoc Neurosensory Analyzer), suprathreshold heat response (quantified through a NRS 0-100), aftersensation, and flexion, extension, right and left range of motion.

Adverse events: A written log of injuries/adverse events 

Follow up: immediately following treatment and at 2 weeks

characteristics.name: Notes
characteristics.value:
Authors' results and conclusions: 'Immediate attenuation of suprathreshold heat response was greatest following SMT (P = .05). Group-dependent differences were not observed for changes in pain intensity and disability at 2 weeks. Participant satisfaction was greatest following the enhanced placebo SMT...The results of this study indicate that attenuation of pain sensitivity is greater in response to SMT than the expectation of receiving SMT. These findings suggest a potential mechanism of SMT related to lessening of central sensitization and may indicate a pre-clinical effect beyond the expectations of receiving SMT.'

Funding source: University of Florida Research Opportunity Fund.
Declarations of interest: The authors acknowledge that they have no conflict of interest or financial involvement with any commercial organization that has a direct interest in any matter included in their manuscript. The principal author received support from the Rehabilitation Research Career Development Program and colleagues received support from the National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine (NCCAM).

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Manual therapy and exercise therapy

  • Description: a single high-velocity manipulation using a side-lying position
  • Non-SMT component: core stabilization exercise program, composed of three sets of specific lumbopelvic exercises
  • Duration/dose: 2 times a week for 12 weeks, 5 minutes of manual therapy, 60 minutes of exercises
  • Treatment provider: physical specialist with eight years of experience

CG1:  Exercise therapy

  • Description: core stabilization exercise program, composed of three sets of specific lumbopelvic exercises
  • Duration/Dose: 2 sets of 24 exercises( static exercise 30 seconds hold and dynamic exercise 10 repetitions) (60 min), 2 times a week for  12 weeks 
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist with 10 years of experience

CG2:  Kinesiotaping and exercise therapy

  • Description: core stabilization exercise program, composed of three sets of specific lumbopelvic exercises. Elastic tape applied to the lower back at the beginning of the sessions and removed after completion of the training program
  • Duration/Dose: 2 sets of 24 exercises( static exercise 30 seconds hold and dynamic exercise 10 repetitions) (60 min), 2 times a week for 12 weeks 
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist with 10 years of experience

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: SMT 

  • Description: 'Spinal manipulative therapy was delivered by nine experienced chiropractors, each of whom determined the frequency and number of treatments for each participant. Visits typically occurred 1 to 2 times per week and lasted 15 to 30 minutes. Short-lever, low-amplitude, high-velocity SMT was applied to specific areas of the low back and sacroiliac regions, identified by assessment of joint motion restriction and pain provocation. Treatment decisions were based on participants’ response to care; treatment plans were modified if there was no change, a worsening of back pain, or dissatisfaction with care. Participants were discharged from care if the treating clinician felt that maximum clinical benefit was obtained.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'Adjunct modalities, limited to a few minutes of soft-tissue massage, ice, or heat, were used to facilitate SMT at the discretion of the chiropractor.'
  • Duration/dose: 'Participants were discharged from care if the treating clinician felt that maximum clinical benefit was obtained. ' Maximum of 12 weeks of care
  • Treatment provider: nine chiropractors

CG1: Supervised exercise therapy 

  • Description: 'Exercises focused on the low back and abdominal musculature, and the program was individualized in terms of intensity (e.g., repetitions and difficulty) according to the patients’ abilities. The delivery method was one-on-one supervision and was considered high dose. The patients perform exercises emphasizing a high number of repetitions and progressive increase in muscle load. The patients performed a series of six static stretches focused on the lumbar, gluteal, and hamstring musculature before and after strengthening. The main focus of the program was dynamic trunk strengthening exercises (trunk extensions and leg extensions) and abdominal exercises using low-tech methods. Three sets of trunk extensions and leg extensions were performed on a stable bench (also known as a Roman chair). Three sets of two types of anterior abdominal exercises were performed: abdominal curl ups on the floor and on a gym ball.'
  • Duration/dose: 'The patients were asked to attend 20, 1-hour sessions (approximately twice per week).'
  • Treatment provider: 15 exercise therapists under the supervision of study clinicians.

CG2: Home exercise and advice 

  • Description: 'Individualized sessions included advice and instruction on self-care measures, such as the use of ice and heat, ergonomic recommendations for home and work, and demonstration of good lifting techniques. Simple stretching and strengthening exercises, including lumbar extension, bridging, and abdominal crunches, were demonstrated and practiced with patient participation. Study participants were given a book and laminated cards describing these exercises and were encouraged to perform them at home on a daily basis. The patients were followed up in person 1 to 2 weeks later and then instructed to continue with the exercises on their own for the remainder of the intervention phase. We considered the program to be of low dose because of the simplicity of the exercises, time required to perform them (2–3 minutes per series), and low number of provider visits.'
  • Duration/dose: two, 1-hour appointments
  • Treatment provider: 11 chiropractors and exercise therapists

Study design: RCT

Statistical analysis: 'the primary outcome was modelled with mixed-effects regression over baseline (the average value obtained at the 2 baseline visits) and 3, 12, 26, and 52 weeks. After assuming that group means were the same at baseline, the additional terms in the model were time (as a categorical variable) and site-bygroup and time-by-group interactions. The site-by-group interaction was removed if it was not significant at the 0.05 level. Because they tested between-group differences at 2 primary endpoints, they used the Bonferroni method to control for 2 tests. The secondary outcome variables were analyzed with the same methods as the primary outcome but without controlling for multiple testing.'

Sample size calculation: 'sample size was calculated to ensure 85% power to detect an 8–percentage point mean difference between groups in patient-rated leg pain; 8 to 11 percentage points have been recommended as a minimally important group difference in pain and disability for LBP studies. They assumed an SD of 17 percentage points and 17% loss to follow-up based on our latest pilot study and a 0.05 level of significance for a 2-tailed test at one endpoint to calculate a target sample size of 96 patients per group.'

characteristics.value:
IG: SMT + home exercise and advice

  • Description: 'For SMT visits, the primary focus of treatment was on manual techniques (including high-velocity, low amplitude thrust procedures or low-velocity, variable amplitude mobilization maneuvers to the lumbar vertebral or sacroiliac joints). The specific spinal level treated and the number and frequency of SMT visits were determined by the clinician on the basis of patient-reported symptoms, palpation, and pain provocation tests.'
  • Non-SMT component: '..attended 4 home exercise and advice visits (see below CG); Adjunct therapies to facilitate SMT were used as needed and included light soft-tissue techniques (that is, active and passive muscle stretching and ischemic compression of tender points) and hot or cold packs.'

  • Treatment provider: 11 chiropractors with a minimum of 5 years of practice experience

CG: Home exercise and advice

  • Description: 'The main program goals were to provide patients with the tools to manage existing pain, prevent pain recurrences, and facilitate engagement in daily activities. Instruction and practice were provided for positioning and stabilization exercises to enhance mobility and increase trunk endurance. These were individualized to patients’ lifestyles, clinical characteristics (including positional sensitivities), and fitness levels. Positioning exercises included extension and flexion motion cycles (patients were encouraged to perform 25 repetitions 3 times per day in the lying, standing, or seated position). Stabilization exercises included pelvic tilt, quadruped, bridging, abdominal curl-ups, and side bridging with positional variations appropriate to patients’ tolerance and abilities. Patients were also instructed in methods for developing spine posture awareness related to their activities of daily living, such as lifting, pushing and pulling, sitting, and getting out of bed. Information about simple pain-management techniques, including cold, heat, and movement, was also provided. Printed materials were distributed to take home and review. They included instructions of exercises with photos and a modification of the Back in Action book, emphasizing movement and restoration of normal function and fitness.'
  • Duration/dose: 'Treatments were delivered in four 1-hour, one-on-one visits during the 12-week intervention. Patients were instructed to do 8 to 12 repetitions of each stabilization exercise every other day.'
  • Treatment provider: delivered by 13 providers (7 chiropractors, 5 exercise therapists, and 1 personal trainer)

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG1: Flexion distraction 

  • Description: 'The flexion-distraction technique applied was modified from Cox’s protocol. Patients were placed in the decubitus prone position on the table, with their umbilicus placed between the dorsal zone of the table and the lumbar body. In this way, anterior superior iliac spines remain placed in the inferior zone of the table. A velcro strap was placed around the ankles. The therapist then used the heel of the hand to contact the upper spinal apophysis at the level to be treated. A modern table with an engine placed under the caudal body was used, which imparts a rhythmic up-and-down movement of the lower limbs in a pumping motion. In each downward movement, the therapist pressed on the L3 lumbar spine vertebra, following the direction towards the table and the patient’s head. In total, there were ten pumping movements, a one-minute pause, a repetition of the previous ten pumping movements, and then another pause, and so on until a total of five minutes were completed. This treatment was repeated during each patient’s visit.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'a 90-second ischemic compression on the four trigger points of the lumbar quadrate muscle and on two trigger points of the iliacus-psoas muscle. Ischemic compression consisted of a digital manual pressure of approximately 90 s. This pressure was enough to leave the skin white but without causing unpleasant pain in patients. Pressure was maintained until relaxation of the trigger point occurred. At that moment, pressure was incremented until a new barrier was found. Then, pressure was maintained again.'
  • Duration/dose: four therapy sessions for two weeks (two sessions per week). This dose has been shown to be effective in providing short-term positive effects. 10 min of therapy.
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist with a degree in osteopathy, ten years’ experience, and chiropractic training 

IG2: HVLA-SMT

  • Description: 'High-velocity spinal manipulation at the low-back level was performed. This treatment was repeated during each patient’s visit. Patients were placed in the lateral decubitus position, keeping upper-level flexion and lumbar spine rotation until the L3-L4 level. The lower limb was passively placed in a triple flexion position. The foot rested on the popliteal space of the opposite inferior limb. In this position, spinal manipulation consisted of an HVLA-SM applied on the inferior level in an anterior and downward direction'
  • Non-SMT component:  'a 90-second ischemic compression on the four trigger points of the lumbar quadrate muscle, and also on two trigger points of the iliacus-psoas muscle. This pressure was enough to leave the skin white but without causing unpleasant pain in patients. Pressure was maintained until relaxation of the trigger point occurred. At that moment, pressure was incremented until a new barrier was found. Then, pressure was maintained again.'
  • Duration/dose:  four therapy sessions for two weeks (two sessions per week). This dose has been shown to be effective in providing short-term positive effects.
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist with a degree in osteopathy, ten years’ experience, and chiropractic training

characteristics.value:
IG: SMT 

  • Description: 'clinicians chose which levels of the spine to manipulate based on the presence of hypomobility (abnormal end-feel and increased tissue resistance) and pain through provocative range of motion testing. The techniques used were: 1. Side-lying pelvic girdle manipulation: the therapist applied a high-velocity low-amplitude thrust intervention of the pelvis in an anterior direction; 2, Side-lying lumbar spine manipulation: the therapist applied a high-velocity low-amplitude thrust intervention of the pelvis in an anterior direction; 3. Thoracic manipulation: A distraction thoracic manipulation in an anterior to posterior direction was applied.   • Description: 'a functional technique intervention targeted at the lumbosacral junction (L5–S1). 'Whereas in classic articular thrust techniques the bone segment is mostly passively corrected (without the patient’s participation), in the functional technique the chiropractor guides the segment through movements, taking into account the response of the tissues, and adapting his or her maneuvers to the tissues without ever forcing them, thereby providing a nontraumatic articular correction. The technique consists of compression of the iliac crests with one hand and caudal traction of the sacrum with the other one. During the technique, the patient performs normal breathing cycles of inspiration and expiration. The technique usually involves 9–10 breathing cycles.'

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: SMT 

  • Description: 'Manipulation was performed by an oblique force which was applied to the inferior lateral angle of the sacrum, taking less than 5 minutes per patient. The technique was carried out as follow: the technique began with the patient side lying with their feet together and their shoulders perpendicular to the stretcher, while the therapist standing at one side of the stretcher near the patient’s pelvis with a slight orientation toward the patient’s head. In that position, an extension and axial traction were made to patient’s lower and upper limbs in contact with the stretcher. A hip and knee flexions were done to the contralateral lower limb, and the therapist did a trunk rotation of the patient toward the ceiling, inducing a slight bend trunk to push posterior the sacral base. The therapist’s pisiform of the caudal hand pressed the patient’s inferior lateral angle (ILA) of the sacrum in contact with the stretcher, while the therapist’s cranial hand stabilized on the groove between the patient’s deltoid and pectoralis major. The barrier was engaged with the therapist's cranial hand contacting the patient's deltopectoral groove and the caudal hand contacting the ILA of the sacrum (the side situated on the stretcher), with the pisiform in the direction of the contralateral shoulder. The thrust was made by a body drop on the rotating pelvis, a mobilization with impulse thrust was provided in a scooping fashion with the caudal hand on the ILA of the sacrum in the direction of the resistant on the contralateral shoulder.'
  • Non-SMT component: none

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Osteopathic manual therapy 

  • Description: 'The treatment protocol only included manual techniques that comprise part of the contemporary osteopathic treatment conduct: articulation and myofascial techniques. Sacroiliac articulation technique: Individual in the ventral position, the therapist standing beside the patient with one hand on the sacral region and the other on the front to stabilize the contact. The therapist will perform a slight compression toward the couch and a movement leading the sacral region in the cranial direction and then in the caudal region, seeking to gain the arc of motion of the nutation, counternutation, anteversion and retroversion movements. Thoracic articulation technique: Individual in the ventral position, therapist beside the couch, with hands placed so that the spinous processes are between them. The therapist performs a compression movement toward the couch, and reverse rotation of the hands during the patient’s exhalation cycles. Performed in all the thoracic vertebrae. Aimed at improving the movement range of the region. '
  • Non-SMT component: 'Stretching technique for lumbar paraspinal muscles: Individual in the dorsal position, with lower limbs in triple flexion. Therapist beside the couch, with one of the hands located under the sacral region of the patient and the other hand on the patient’s feet. The therapist performs rhythmic movements while simultaneously lifting the lower limbs in the cranial direction of the patient and lifting the sacrum in the caudal direction, aiming for relaxation of the lumbar paraspinal muscles. Lumbar myofascial technique: Participant in the ventral position, therapist beside the couch in direction perpendicular to the participant with one hand splayed on the lower back of the patient to the side of the spinous processes and perpendicular to the muscle fibers of the region, the other hand on the front to give stabilization. The therapist performs perpendicular slides in the direction of the muscle fibers. Performing 15 repetitions on each side, aiming for a generalized lumbar muscle relaxation.'
  • Duration/dose: session lasted between 30-45 min. The osteopathic manipulation treatment was conducted once a week for a total of five weeks, with a total of 5 treatment sessions
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist with a graduate degree in Osteopathy

  • Description: Maitland joint mobilisation or manipulation techniques
  • Non-SMT component: participants were not given exercises or a home exercise program and were advised to avoid pain-aggravating activities.

CG1: General exercise 

  • Description: 'The aim was to improve physical functioning and confidence in using the spine, and to teach participants to cope with their back problems. The class was modeled on the 'Back to fitness' program described by Klabber-Moffet and Frost.'
  • Duration/Dose: exercises were performed in classes of up to 8 people. Each class lasts approximately 1 hour. The intensity of the exercises progressed over the 12 treatments
  • Treatment provider: supervision of a physical therapist 

CG2: Motor control exercise

  • Description: 'The aim was to improve the function of specific trunk muscles thought to control the movement of the spine and to recruit the deep muscles of the spine and reduce the activity of other muscles. Initially, participants were taught how to contract the transversus abdominis and multifidus muscles in isolation from the more superficial trunk muscles, but in conjunction with the pelvic floor muscles. Ultrasonography was used to provide feedback about muscle recruitment. Both exercise groups also received cognitive-behavioral therapy. This was designed to encourage skill acquisition by modeling, the use of pacing, setting progressive goals, self-monitoring of progress, and positive reinforcement of progress. Self-reliance was fostered by encouraging participants to engage in problem-solving to deal with difficulties rather than seeking reassurance and advice, by encouraging relevant activity goals, and by encouraging self-reinforcement.'
  • Duration/dose: 12 treatment sessions over an 8-week period, except for the SMT group, who were allowed to discontinue if they recovered.
  • Treatment Provider: Each participant was trained by a physical therapist

characteristics.name: Methods
characteristics.value:
Study design: RCT

Recruitment period: from February 2017 to June 2018

Statistical analysis: 'the analysis of variance (ANOVA) test for repeated measures was used to compare numerical variables. The factors analyzed were group and time (pre and postintervention). Tests of within-patient post hoc simple effects (i.e. changes in time for all variables for each group separately) were performed by post hoc Bonferroni corrections.'

Sample size calculation: Calculations were based on a minimal detectable change of 15 mm on the VAS in patients with low back pain. Assuming a standard deviation of 16.18 mm, two-tailed tests, and an alpha level of 0.5, a sample size of 42 participants was generated for the study in order to have 90% power to identify an effect. Allowing for a dropout rate of 20%, we planned to recruit at least 49 patients.

Inclusion criteria

Exclusion criteria

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Non Thrust Manipulation

  • Description: 'Patients received a semi-standardised approach targeting the symptomatic level in the lumbar spine. The technique and grade of the NTM were at the clinician's discretion and based on the findings from the clinical examination. The number of bouts and duration of each bout for the NTM were standardised to include three bouts performed for 45 s with 45 s in between.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'A standardized Home Exercise Programme (HEP) consisting of mobility and stabilization exercises of the lumbopelvic area was reviewed at their initial visit. Each participant was asked to complete the program one time per day during his or her participation in the trial. Adherence was monitored using an exercise log with a threshold set at 80% considered successful.'
  • Duration/dose: two visits per week for three weeks totaling six visits
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist

CG: Dry needling

  • Description: 'Fifty millimeters (mm)/.25 gauge Seirin J-type needles were inserted to the maximum or available depth at each location. Segmental DN involved needling the paraspinal levels and then distally into peripheral nerve innervation fields of the lower extremity. Two needles were placed along bilateral lumbar paraspinal muscles at the symptomatic level, a level above, and a level below. Needles were then inserted into both lower extremities targeting peripheral nerve distributions. Needling distal to the primary site of pain reduces neural sensitivity by attenuating the spinal reflex arc. Twenty-two needles were used each visit, and total treatment time ranged between 5 and 7 min depending on patient tolerance. See Figure 1. No needle manipulation was performed other than slight modifications needed to reach the 50 mm or maximum available depth. Once all needles were inserted, the therapist removed them. In addition, the patient performed the same HEP as in the intervention group. '
  • Duration/dose: two visits per week for three weeks totaling six visits.
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist

characteristics.value:
IG1: 18 SMT sessions only

  • Description: '18 sessions of manual thrust (high-velocity, low-amplitude) spinal manipulation in the lumbar and transition thoracic regions, predominantly in the side-posture position. Specific manipulations to be performed were determined at each visit by the chiropractor through ongoing evaluation of the participants including patient progress, self-reported and provocative pain, spinal range of motion, and palpation of the spine and paraspinal soft tissue. Manipulation was not performed at a visit if the treating chiropractor failed to find any indication. Lighter thrust manipulation including the use of mechanical assistance of a spring-loaded table and segmental low-velocity mobilisation was permitted in the case of acute exacerbation of the lumbar spine pain.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'Participants received a hot pack for 5 minutes to relax spinal muscles followed by 5 minutes for the SMT or control intervention.'

 IG 2: 12 SMT + 6 Light massage

  • Description: 12 sessions of manual thrust (high-velocity, low-amplitude) spinal manipulation in the lumbar and transition thoracic regions, predominantly in the side-posture position.

The massage used was gentler and of shorter duration than recommended for therapeutic massage practice. As such, it was a minimalist intervention to control touching the patient. Participants received a hot pack for 5 minutes to relax spinal muscles followed by 5 minutes for the SMT or control intervention.'

 IG3: 6 SMT + 12 Light massage

The massage used was gentler and of shorter duration than recommended for therapeutic massage practice. As such, it was a minimalist intervention to control touching the patient. characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Bone-setting

  • Description: 'The bone-setters were free to choose the methods from their repertoires. The method they most commonly applied was the gentle mobilisation of the spine. The patient sits on a stool with the therapist behind him. The therapist first uses his fingers to find out if the spinous processes are in line or “dislocated” up or down or on either side. If a vertebra is found to be “out of alignment,” the patient is asked to bend forward and slowly straighten up while the therapist holds his thumbs against the transverse processes of the next lower vertebra, thus presumably mobilizing the upper facet joints. Another common method is simply to rub the “misaligned” spinous processes gently from all sides to “negotiate” them into a “correct position.” The massage was applied occasionally. No direct and forceful, “chiropractic” manipulations were used. The 2002 report states that this therapy is consistent with chiropractic or osteopathy.' [Note: Comment reviewers: In the 1997 report, it explicitly states that no direct or forceful 'chiropractic' manipulations were used, while the 2002 report states that bone setting is consistent with chiropractic or osteopathy].
  • Non-SMT component: None
  • Duration/dose: A maximum 10 1-hour sessions of each therapy was offered; 6-week treatment program. The mean number of treatments was 8.1 (2.7)
  • Treatment provider: delivered by 4 folk healers aged 40 to 70 years with a practical experience of up to 30 years, but with no formal medical education

CG1: Physiotherapy

  • Description: 'a combination of manual, thermal, and electrotherapy. The therapist was free to choose a suitable method within these categories and to use the facilities at his disposal: hot/cold packs, infrared heat, ultrasound, shortwave diathermy, and transcutaneous electric nerve stimulation. In addition to massage, he also employed specific mobilisations and manual traction according to the GP’s prescription, but no manipulations with impulse. Individual auto-stretching exercises were added if indicated. The physiotherapy group. was allowed to perform specific mobilisations, but not manipulations with impulse.'
  • Duration/dose: A maximum of 10 1-hour sessions of each therapy was offered; 6-week treatment program. The mean number of treatments was 9.9 (0.7)
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist 

CG2: Home exercises with individual instruction by physiotherapist (N = 35):

  • Description: 'patients were taught a constant program: to bend their low back rhythmically from side to side and back and forth as well as to rotate from side to side, ten times in each direction every 1.5 minutes, whenever sitting, standing, or lying still (e.g., watching TV, driving a car) or at least before getting up in the morning and after lying down in the evening.' The program also included 10 sit-up, 10 arch-up, and 10 trunk rotation exercises twice a day.
  • Duration/dose: A maximum 10 1-hour sessions of each therapy was offered; 6-week treatment program. The mean number of treatments was 4.5 (2.2)
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist

A study nurse first registered and interviewed the patients, obtained a written consent, and finally randomised the patients by drawing sealed lots after a general practitioner had completed the baseline clinical examinations and measurements. The nurse also delivered the questionnaires and booked the follow-up therapy sessions, keeping the general practitioner strictly blind to the randomised therapies

Note: this detailed information was found in the follow-up study; information on the randomisation procedure were lacking in the original 1997 study.
No published protocol was available; disability and recovery were not reported.
There were no significant important differences between the four groups in terms of these baseline characteristics and outcomes

Patients were advised in the beginning not to take any therapy other than that to which they were randomised. One patient (3%) from the physiotherapy group had consulted a physiotherapist and 8 (24%) a bonesetter. During follow-up one patient from the exercise group was operated on for a herniated disc and one from the bone-setting group was referred to a rehabilitation center.

From the 1997 publication: 41% of the physiotherapy, 58% of the bone-setting, and 44% of the exercise patients took some form of therapy during the follow-up period (comment: unclear what this therapy consisted of and whether it was therapy other than to which the patients were randomised); however, the authors state in the discussion that '... the exercise and the physiotherapy patients tended to switch over to bone-setting after the 6-week treatment period.'

76% of the physiotherapy patients (N = 26/34), 89% of the bone-setting patients (N = 40/45), and 57% of the exercise patients (N = 20/35) did not seek other therapy to which they were randomised.

Half of the exercise patients reported having done at least three quarters of the required home exercises during the 6-week treatment period. After 3 months 32 exercise patients (80%), and after 6 months 19 (54%), still reported having continued the exercises, while 4 (11%) had physiotherapy and 8 (23%) bone-setting therapy. Twelve bone-setting patients (27%) had continued on bone-setting and 3 (7%) had received physiotherapy.
Identical per group

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG1: High-velocity low-amplitude SMT 

  • Description: 'side-lying diversified lumbar spine “adjustment” or maneuver. Participants were positioned in a lateral recumbent or side-lying position with the superior or free hip and knee flexed and adducted across the midline. The intent of the SMT was to isolate one or more vertebral segments. The impulse load was delivered by a quick, short, controlled movement of the shoulder, arm and hand combined with a slight body drop.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'During week 3, the chiropractor provider delivered 30 minutes of standardized instructions for a home exercise program to all participants enrolled in the trial. The exercise prescription guidelines were tailored to individual participant ability and instructed participants to begin an aerobic program as well as low-back stretching and strengthening exercises. Participants were given a handout with pictures of 7 low-back exercises, with the number of sets and repetitions tailored and delineated for each participant.'
  • Duration/dose: 12 visits (not to exceed 3 times per week for the first 2 weeks, 2 times per week for the third and fourth weeks, and once per week during weeks 5 and 6)
  • Treatment provider: 4 chiropractors and all had more than 6 years practice experience

IG2: Low-Velocity Variable Amplitude Spinal mobilisation

  • Description: 'Flexion-distraction technique or Cox technique. Participants were positioned prone on a treatment table that was designed to allow free but controllable motion to the lower half of the participant's body. The distal section of the table also allowed the chiropractor to apply traction to the lumbar spine. During this maneuver, the intent was to stabilize a specific vertebra by applying anterior to posterior and cephalad pressure to the spinous process. Simultaneously, the chiropractor moved the lower mobile portion of the table through the ranges of motion normal to the human spine.'
  • Non-SMT component: 'In addition, during week 3, the chiropractor delivered 30 minutes of standardized instructions for a home exercise program to all participants enrolled in the trial. The exercise prescription guidelines were tailored to individual participant ability and instructed participants to begin an aerobic program as well as low-back stretching and strengthening exercises. Participants were given a handout with pictures of 7 low-back exercises, with the number of sets and repetitions tailored and delineated for each participant.'
  • Duration/dose: 12 visits (not to exceed 3 times per week for the first 2 weeks, 2 times per week for the third and fourth weeks, and once per week during weeks 5 and 6)
  • Treatment provider:  4 chiropractors and all had more than 6 years practice experience

CG: Medical care

  • Description: 'All participants were scheduled to attend visits at weeks 3 and 6 to be evaluated by the medical provider and complete questionnaires. Additional visits were scheduled at the discretion of the medical provider. The goal of pain management was improvement in pain and optimisation of activities of daily living. The first option was paracetamol (acetaminophen), followed by NSAIDs and muscle relaxants. In addition, during week 3, the medical physician delivered 30 minutes of standardized instructions for a home exercise program to all participants enrolled in the trial. The exercise prescription guidelines were tailored to individual participant ability and instructed participants to begin an aerobic program as well as low-back stretching and strengthening exercises. Participants were given a handout with pictures of 7 low-back exercises, with the number of sets and repetitions tailored and delineated for each participant.'
  • Duration/dose: 3 visits of medical care.
  • Treatment provider:  1 medical physician board-certified in neurology and had more than 10 years practice experience

Adverse events: 23 patients reported adverse effects from the treatments: 7 in the combined group, 6 in the joint manipulation group, 4 in the myofascial therapy group, and 6 in the back school group. These adverse effects were mostly transient exacerbations of symptoms, except for one case of constant tinnitus in the myofascial therapy group. Two of the patients claimed that treatment (joint manipulation) had aggravated their conditions. Both received conservative care at no charge after 3 weeks of therapy and were released when their pain became stabilized.

Follow-up: at 3 weeks and 6 months

characteristics.name: Methods
characteristics.value:
Study design: RCT

Recruitment period: from May 1996 to June 1998

Statistical analysis: 'the analyses were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) on the four groups, with contrasts for comparisons of individual groups. In some cases, analyses were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Tukey test.'

Sample size calculation: recruitment was not successful ('recruitment goal was 300 patients').

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: After acceptance into the study, patients were randomised into one of four treatment groups using a computer program designed to balance allocation of patients according to age, gender, duration of LBP, and treatment preference for physical therapy or chiropractic. Randomization was performed separately at each site.

No other information was provided, e.g. whether the person who performed the allocation was an independent examiner; whether consecutively numbered, sealed opaque envelopes were used during allocation, etc.
No published protocol available; pain and functional status were measured.
There were no significant important differences between the four groups in terms of these baseline characteristics and outcomes (see table 1 and 2).

During the 3-week trial period, only a minor proportion of the patients (10%) reported use of over-the-counter pain medications (e.g., ibuprofen, acetaminophen). Six patients reported eight visits to health care practitioners. Among these, two visits were related to LBP. Therefore, treatment contamination was insignificant.

After 3 weeks of therapy, 12 patients reported continuing care for LBP: 5 patients in the combined therapy group, 1 patient in the joint manipulation group, 3 patients in the myofascial therapy group, and 3 patients in the back school group. Altogether, 33 visits were reported: 16 visits in the combined therapy group, 1 visit in the joint manipulation group, 13 visits in the myofascial therapy group, and 3 visits in the back school group. During the study, 18 health care practitioners were consulted: 8 chiropractors, 5 medical doctors, 2 physical therapists, 1 osteopath, 1 acupuncturist, and 1 foot reflexologist.

Disconcordant compliance across the different therapies.

Full compliance was noted for 90% (47/52) treated patients in the combined therapy group, 88% (43/49) treated patients in the joint manipulation group, 92% (47/51) treated patients in the myofascial therapy group, and 69% (33/48) treated patients in the back school group. The back school group was the least compliant.
After 3 weeks of treatment and at 6 months follow-up.

Authors' results and conclusions: The mean changes in LBP intensity and disability of participants in the medical and chiropractic care-only groups were similar at each follow-up assessment. Physical therapy yielded somewhat better 6-month disability outcomes than did medical care alone. After 6 months of follow-up, chiropractic care and medical care for LBP were comparable in their effectiveness. Physical therapy may be marginally more effective than medical care alone for reducing disability in some patients, but the possible benefit is small.

IG1: Chiropractic care only

  • Description: spinal manipulation or another spinal-adjusting technique (e.g., mobilisation), instruction in strengthening and flexibility exercises, and instruction in proper back care. Chiropractic practice at the study site is consistent with chiropractic philosophy and training throughout the USA. The chiropractors routinely used the diversified technique, which is the general type of spinal manipulation taught in most chiropractic schools and is the most frequently used form of manipulation.
  • Non-SMT component: instruction in strengthening and flexibility exercises, and instruction in proper back care
  • Duration/dose: Frequency of chiropractic visits were at the discretion of chiropractor assigned to the patient
  • Treatment provider: chiropractor

IG2: Chiropractic care with physical modalities

  • Treatment provider: chiropractor 

CG1: Medical care only

  • Description: consisted of one or more of the following at the discretion of the medical provider: instruction in proper back care and strengthening and flexibility exercises; prescriptions for pain killers, muscle relaxants, anti-inflammatory agents, and other medications used to reduce or eliminate pain or discomfort; and recommendations regarding bedrest, weight loss, and physical activities.

  • Treatment provider: a medical provider

CG2: Medical care with physical therapy

  • Description: Patients assigned to this group received medical care as described above, instruction in proper back care from the physical therapist, plus one or more of the following at the discretion of the physical therapist: heat therapy, cold therapy, ultrasound, electrical muscle stimulation (EMS), soft-tissue and joint mobilisation, traction, supervised therapeutic exercise, and strengthening and flexibility exercises.

characteristics.name: Methods
characteristics.value:
Study design: RCT

Recruitment period: from October 1995 to November 1998

Statistical analysis: three analytic strategies were used to estimate treatment effects: 1) ordinary least squares regression models were used to estimate differences in mean change on each continuous outcome variable from baseline to each follow-up assessment; 2) logistic regression was used to estimate and test the effects of treatments on dichotomous outcomes; and 3) mixed effects linear models were used to show changes in each outcome over the 6-month follow-up period by treatment group.

Sample size calculation: not reported

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: The study statistician ran a computer program to generate randomised assignments in blocks of 12, stratified by site. The statistician placed each treatment assignment in a numbered security envelope. A separate series of sequentially numbered sealed envelopes was provided for each of the three sites.

When each patient consented to be in the study, the field coordinator opened the site-specific envelope in sequence and documented the patient for whom the assignment was made and the time of the assignment.
No published protocol, but all primary outcomes (pain, functional status, and recovery) were reported.
There were no significant important differences between the four groups in terms of these baseline characteristics and outcomes

Approximately 20% of patients in the chiropractic groups received concurrent medical care, whereas 7% of patients in the medical groups received concurrent chiropractic care in the first 6 weeks. None of the chiropractic patients assigned to the chiropractic grp. only also received physical therapy, as opposed to approximately 3% of the medical patients assigned to receive medical care only who also received physical therapy.

The specific therapies received by patients varied within each treatment group and the study protocol did not prescribe the type or amount of care that should be received by participating patients. Frequency of medical and chiropractic visits were at the discretion of the medical provider or chiropractor. Frequency of physical therapy visits was at the discretion of the supervising physical therapist.

Ninety-nine percent of patients had at least one visit to their assigned chiropractic or medical provider; however, about one-third of patients randomly assigned to medical care with physical therapy had no physical therapy visits.
Identical per group

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG: Manipulation

  • Description: Supine SIJ manipulation: 'The therapist stood opposite to the side of SIJ dysfunction and moved the patient onto his or her side, leaning toward the side of SIJ dysfunction. Then the therapist rotated the patient toward himself and delivered a quick posterolateral and inferior thrust through the anterior superior iliac spine. Side-lying SIJ manipulation (anterior rotation): The patient lay on his or her side with the dysfunction side up, and the therapist stood in front. The therapist applied flexion to the top of the lower extremity and rotated the trunk toward the opposite side (the trunk posteriorly and the pelvis anteriorly), until movement was felt at the lumbosacral junction. Then the top foot was placed in the lower popliteal space. While stabilizing the trunk and forearm in the ischial region, the therapist applied thrust to the pelvis. Side-lying SIJ manipulation (posterior rotation): As in the above technique, but the therapist stood near the patient's forearm posterior to the region of the iliac bone, and applied thrust to the pelvis.'
  • Non-SMT component: In the first or second sessions in both treatment groups, medication was used under supervision of their physician if a patient had severe pain.
  • Duration/dose: three times a week for two weeks
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist expert in manual therapy with six years' experience

CG: Stabilization exercise

  • Description: 'In the first session the patients were told how to find and maintain control of neutral spine alignment both in the lumbo- pelvic region and in relation to the thorax and hip joint. During the second and third sessions the patients were taught to consciously recruit tonic, low intensity isolated contractions (15%-20% of maximum voluntary contraction) of the local stabilizers of the lumbopelvic region to ensure segmental control in different posi- tions (e.g. supine, crook-lying, side-lying, prone, four-point kneeling, sitting and standing).  The goal was co-contraction of the local muscles [transverse abdominis (TA) and deep fibers of multifidus (MF)] with normal breathing patterns. Contraction of the TA and MF was monitored by palpating just medial and inferior to the anterior superior iliac spines, and lateral to the spinous process of the lumbar spine or sacrum bilaterally, respectively. The exercises were gradually intensified in subsequent sessions by applying low loads to the muscles through the upper and lower limbs and thoracopelvic movement in different positions, and then based on proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation patterns with an elastic resistance band. In the two final stages the patients were trained in how to move from the neutral spine position to other positions, which is essential for stability during many functional activities (e.g. sitting up, rotating the pelvis or upper trunk). The patients were also taught how to use the contraction of local muscles during daily activities.'
  • Duration/dose: All patients exercised for 20 min three times a week, for four weeks. In this group the maximum number of sessions that could be completed was 12 sessions. However, the actual number of completed sessions was from 8 to 12, depending on when complete improvement was observed. Exercises in each position were performed in 10 repetitions
  • Treatment provider: physiotherapist with expertise in the training of stabilization exercises and seven years’ experience

Contamination and co-interventions mainly occurred among patients in the placebo and general practitioner grp. Seven patients in the placebo grp. received physiotherapy before the 3-week follow-up; one due to an administrative error, one due to unmasking of the placebo by the patient, and 5 because the therapist decided that giving the placebo was not appropriate for the patient in question.

4 patients in the GP grp. received physiotherapy or manual therapy before the 3-week follow-up; one because the patient did not want treatment by the GP, one because the GP carried out manual therapy himself, and two because the GP thought that a referral was more appropriate.

In the physiotherapy and manual therapy grp., these changes occurred considerably less often.

characteristics.name: Methods
characteristics.value:
Study design: RCT

Recruitment period: from January 2000 to February 2001

Statistical analysis: 'Analysis of variance was used to test for differences among the groups in continuous variables, and the chi-2 test was used for dichotomous or categorical variables.'

Sample size calculation: not clear if recruitment was successful because it wasn't explicitly stated ('The numbers of subjects receiving OMT and not receiving OMT (the latter including the sham manipulation subjects and the no-intervention control subjects combined) to be included in the trial to achieve a power of approximately 80% in detecting moderate to large differences between groups were determined using the SF-36 scales. The latter were used because they comprised the majority of primary outcomes...').

risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Randomization was performed using sequential sealed envelopes prepared by the clinical research technician before enrolment of the subjects. The subjects were assigned randomly to one of three treatment groups in an approximate 2:1:1 ratio: OMT, sham manipulation, or no intervention as a control condition. The intent of this allocation strategy was to enrol comparable numbers of subjects receiving OMT and not receiving OMT, and subsequently to combine the sham manipulation and no-intervention control groups should no statistically significant differences be observed between the latter groups.

The treating pre-doctoral osteopathic manipulative medicine fellows subsequently opened the sealed envelopes and recorded the allocation of subjects as they entered the trial. All trial personnel with the exception of the osteopathic fellows were blinded to treatment group assignments throughout the trial. Note: Unclear, but appears that those who determined allocation were also involved in the actual treatment.

(According to the authors) 14 primary outcomes: Pain (10-cm VAS); Back-pain specific functional status: Roland-Morris; SF-36 (8 sub-scales, incl. physical functioning, role limitations - physical & emotional, bodily pain, general health, vitality, social functioning, and mental health); number of co-treatments, current back pain-specific medication use, lost work or school days related to back pain, and global satisfaction with back care. Recovery was not reported.

No published protocol was available and the authors note 14 primary outcomes, thus no a priori decision was made regarding which were primary and secondary, leading to potential reporting bias of those outcomes that were significant.
Allocation resulted in baseline comparability between groups. Also, the baseline data for outcomes was similar between the groups

All the subjects, regardless of group assignment, were allowed to receive usual or other low-back care to complement the trial interventions, with the exception of other OMT or chiropractic manipulation. Data were collected on each subject’s use of co-treatments throughout the trial including prescription and over-the-counter medications, physical therapy, massage therapy, hydrotherapy, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, spinal and epidural injections, acupuncture, herbal therapies, and meditation. However, the OMT subjects used significantly fewer co-treatments than the no-intervention control subjects at 6 months. There were no significant differences among the treatment groups in back-pain specific medication use or lost work or school days over time.

(Comment: Co-intervention use was assessed only at baseline, 1 and 6 months, asking about such use during the 4 previous weeks. The 1-month assessment probably did not provide sufficient time following randomisation to make appointments with clinicians, clinics, hospitals, etc. outside the trial protocol. Whereas by 6 months, subjects had more time to acquire such co-treatments (personal communication with the primary author).)
Unclear if (or what percentage of) the subjects assigned to OMT or sham manipulation attended the number or sessions prescribed in the methods.
Identical per group

Inclusion criteria

  • Between 21 and 69 years of age
  • Give a positive response to the screening item, 'Have you had low back pain constantly or on most days for the last three months?'
  • Identify low back as the primary site of pain
  • Agree to forego any type of extra-trial manipulation (either chiropractic or osteopathic) or physical therapy
  • Understand and complete trial questionnaires in English, or, if available, with appropriate translation services for other languages
  • Give written informed consent for clinical screening and, if selected, for trial participation
  • Not be pregnant or plan to become pregnant during the course of the trial

Exclusion criteria

  • History of any of the following conditions which may be underlying causes of low back symptoms: (a) cancer; (b) spinal osteomyelitis; (c) spinal fracture; (d) herniated disc; (e) ankylosing spondylitis; (f) cauda equina syndrome
  • History of surgery involving the low back within the past year or planned low back surgery in the future; 
  • History of receiving Worker's Compensation benefits within the past three months
  • Involvement in current litigation relating to back problems
  • Current pregnancy or plan to become pregnant during the course of the trial
  • Any of the following that may limit a treatment provider's choice of OMT techniques or hamper a subject's compliance with the trial protocol: (a) angina or congestive heart failure symptoms that occur at rest or with minimal activity; or (b) history of a stroke or transient ischemic attack within the past year
  • Any of the following that may represent potential contraindications to receiving UPT: (a) implantation of a cardiac pacemaker; (b) implantation of artificial joints or other biomedical devices; (c) active bleeding or infection in the low back; or (d) pregnancy
  • Use of intravenous, intramuscular, or oral corticosteroids within the past month
  • History of chiropractic manipulation, OMT, or UPT within the past three months or on more than three occasions during the past year
  • Being an osteopathic physician, allopathic physician, chiropractor, or physical therapist (or student of any of these professions)

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG1: OMT and UPT

  • Description: 'consisted of high-velocity, low-amplitude thrusts; moderate velocity, moderate-amplitude thrusts; soft tissue stretching, kneading, and pressure; myofascial stretching and release; positional treatment of myofascial tender points; and muscle energy techniques.'
  • Non-SMT component: Ultrasound physical therapy: used normally in physical medicine and rehabilitation programs for musculoskeletal disorders. Aside from the assigned active or sham OMT intervention (and acquiescence to avoid any other forms of manual therapy), patients could use any LBP self-care modalities and receive any other LBP co-treatments from practitioners of their choice.
  • Duration/dose: six treatment sessions were provided at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8, and an exit visit at week 12
  • Treatment provider: osteopath

IG2: OMT + Sham UPT

  • Description: OMT as described above
  • Non-SMT component: Sham ultrasound (UPT): Sub-therapeutic ultrasound will be provided by setting the ultrasound unit to 0.1 W/cm2 intensity at 1 MHz; however, the applicator head will be applied directly to the subject's skin in the low back using ultrasonic conductivity gel to simulate in all other respects the actual UPT maneuvers described above. Aside from the assigned active or sham OMT intervention (and acquiescence to avoid any other forms of manual therapy), patients could use any LBP self-care modalities and receive any other LBP co-treatments from practitioners of their choice.
  • Duration/dose: six treatment sessions were provided at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8, and an exit visit at week 12
  • Treatment provider: osteopath 

CG1: Sham OMT + UPT

  • Description:  simulated these techniques, but with improper patient positioning, purposely misdirected movements, and diminished treatment provider force. It also provided an active and passive range of motion.
  • Non-SMT component: UPT as described above. Aside from the assigned active or sham OMT intervention (and acquiescence to avoid any other forms of manual therapy), patients could use any LBP self-care modalities and receive any other LBP co-treatments from practitioners of their choice.
  • Duration/dose: six treatment sessions were provided at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8, and an exit visit at week 12
  • Treatment provider: osteopath

CG2: Sham OMT + Sham UPT

  • Description: Sham OMT as described and Sham UPT as described. Aside from the assigned active or sham OMT intervention (and acquiescence to avoid any other forms of manual therapy), patients could use any LBP self-care modalities and receive any other LBP co-treatments from practitioners of their choice.
  • Duration/dose: six treatment sessions were provided at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8, and an exit visit at week 12

  • If they reported: a recent low back surgery; a receipt of worker’s compensation benefits ts or ongoing litigation involving back problems; medical conditions that might impede osteopathic manual treatment or Kaltenborn- Evjenth Ortopedic Manual Therapy protocol implementation; corticosteroid taking during the past month; taking a manual therapy during the past three months or more than three times during the past year

characteristics.name: Interventions
characteristics.value:
IG1: Osteopathic manual treatment

  • Description: Osteopathic manual treatment techniques. HVLA impulse. 'The position for lumbar spine manipulation is very similar to that used during sacroiliac joint techniques. The patient is placed in a lateral recumbent position, and the therapist tries to isolate the area to be manipulated by stabilization of the spinous process of the lumbar vertebra. The joint is then stressed to its end range of motion with the therapist’s forearm placed over the ischial tuberosity. At that point, a high-velocity, low-amplitude impulse is applied. An alternate technique is to place the hypothenar eminence on the paraspinal tissues and again stress the joint to its end range of motion. A high-velocity, low-amplitude impulse is then applied as in the first type of application.'
  • Non-SMT component: Strain counter strain myofascial release and visceral mobilisation techniques.
  • Duration/dose: All participants received two treatments weekly for five weeks. No session in either group exceeded 30 minutes. During each session, osteopathic manual treatment and Kaltenborn-Evjenth orthopedic manual therapy techniques were repeated 3 times.
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist

IG2: Kaltenborn-Evjenth orthopedic manual therapy

  • Description: Lumbar segmental traction. 'The patient is in the right, lateral, recumbent position with his or her knees flexed above the level of the abdomen. The physician’s fingers hook over the proximal transverse processes or in the soft tissues of the proximal paravertebral area. Then the physician’s fingers pull the surface in the opposite directions while applying counterpressure using his or her thigh or thighs against the patient’s knees.Lumbar segmental flexion mobilization. The patient is lying on his or her side on a bed, with bent hip joints and knee joints. While facing the patient, the therapist places his or her right hand (fixed hand) on the patient’s lumbar vertebrae, with fingers fixed on the vertebra’s transverse or spinous process.The therapist’s left hand (moving hand) is placed on the patient’s sacral vertebrae, with fingers placed on the vertebra’s transverse or spinous process. The therapist’s chest is put into tight contact with the patient’s two knee joints to move the patient’s pelvis in a caudal or ventral direction.'
  • Non-SMT component: not reported
  • Duration/dose: All participants received two treatments weekly for five weeks. No session in either group exceeded 30 minutes. During each session, osteopathic manual treatment and Kaltenborn-Evjenth orthopedic manual therapy techniques were repeated 3 times.
  • Treatment provider: physical therapist
